articles.standfirst: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso responde al expresidente de la Generalitat en redes
articles.summary: El portavoz de ERC en el Congreso responde al expresidente de la Generalitat en redes
articles.body: Gabriel Rufián, portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados, ha respondido a Carles Puigdemont, expresidente de la Generalitat, en redes sociales. El dirigente de Junts ha criticado la, según su criterio, manipulación informativa en la votación de la ley de los grupos de interés. "La manipulación informativa de las redes es difícil de controlar, pero la de los medios públicos no. Ocultar y distorsionar la realidad para alimentar un determinado relato partidista es inaceptable, es indecente y quita toda la credibilidad al medio", ha publicado Puigdemont en su cuenta de X, antes Twitter. Por su parte, Gabriel Rufián le ha respondido directamente, en la misma plataforma, citando su mensaje: "Votasteis con el PP y VOX de forma reiterada contra el pueblo de Cataluña y a favor de los intereses de la patronal y del lobby inmobiliario. No es relato, es la verdad. Y simplemente ya no tenéis el poder de taparlo. Solo merecéis el más absoluto ostracismo". La tensión en redes sociales entre el portavoz de ERC y Junts es habitual. El Congreso de los Diputados ha votado en contra de la ley de 'lobbies'. Concretamente, PP, Vox, Junts y UPN han votado en contra y PNV y Podemos se han abstenido en el proceso. Sumar, inicialmente, se disponía a votar que no, pero finalmente ha votado sí, menos tres diputados que se han abstenido. Además, Aina Vidal, su portavoz, había emitido, previamente, un voto telemático en contra. La votación se ha cerrado con 179 votos en contra, 155 a favor y 12 abstenciones. Según ha explicado Miriam Nogueras en redes sociales, Junts ha votado en contra de la ley de 'lobbies' por el siguiente motivo: "Junts no vota a favor porque es una ley que ahoga a pequeñas asociaciones y entidades catalanas poniéndolas en el mismo saco que a las grandes empresas del IBEX. Los fondos europeos (1.500 millones) que han quedado en el aire se suman a muchos otros que los socialistas ya han dejado perder".

articles.title: Tim Scott opens up on ‘miraculous’ car crash survival that changed the course of his life
articles.summary: Tim Scott told Sean Hannity he yelled "Jesus" during the crash that sent him through a windshield and derailed several college football scholarships.
articles.body: Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., opened up about the car crash that derailed his football dreams as a teenager, revealing the moment he believes divine intervention saved his life. "I called for help, which for me was, I just yelled, 'Jesus,'" the South Carolina Republican recalled during the latest episode of "Hang Out With Sean Hannity." "I feel like, in an unusually miraculous way, some power — angel, in my opinion — protected me through all of that carnage." REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG Scott recounted the crash during a conversation with Fox News host Sean Hannity at last week’s Republican National Committee Midterm Convention in Dallas, where the two discussed the pivotal moment in the senator's life that unfolded long before he entered national politics. Scott, a standout high school football player at the time, had been "moving up the ranks" when the crash derailed his athletic career. He recalled driving his mother to work one morning before falling asleep behind the wheel on his way home. COLTON BURPO DESCRIBES MEETING JESUS AND HEARING ANGELS SING DURING NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE After waking to the sound of his tires on gravel, Scott said he slammed on the brakes and jerked the steering wheel, sending the car spinning across lanes of traffic before it hit the median. The impact sent him through the windshield as he held onto the steering wheel. The crash left Scott with a broken ankle and back injuries, and many promises of college athletic scholarships dwindled. Presbyterian College in Clinton, South Carolina, however, offered Scott a partial scholarship. He said he later gave his life and heart to Jesus Christ while attending a Fellowship of Christian Athletes (FCA) meeting at the school. articles.title: Leaked Trump plan sparks GOP showdown over how far Republicans should go to support families
articles.summary: The Trump admin's $9,000 stay-at-home parent proposal sparks a fierce conservative divide, with some critics calling it socialism and a slippery slope.
articles.body: The Trump administration is reportedly floating a plan to let some married families with a stay-at-home parent tap federal childcare dollars — a proposal that has triggered a growing fight among conservatives over how far Washington should go to support family life. The reported proposal would expand eligibility for Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) assistance to some married families in which one spouse works at least 35 hours a week and the other stays home, with the benefit averaging about $9,000 per child annually, according to reports. The New York Times reported Sept. 5 that the administration was considering the proposal in the context of Vice President JD Vance’s long-standing advocacy for extending childcare assistance to stay-at-home parents, although a White House official told Fox News Digital that Vance has not pushed this specific proposal. AMERICA’S CHILD CARE CRISIS NEEDS MORE PARENTAL FREEDOM — NOT MORE WASHINGTON CONTROL "Until the administration officially unveils a policy push, any leaked reporting about potential policy ideas that have been neither fully baked nor released should be regarded as pointless speculation," said the official. The Child Care and Development Block Grant was enacted in 1990 under President George H.W. Bush, and the 1996 welfare overhaul under President Bill Clinton amended the program and integrated it with mandatory childcare funding streams that are now commonly known as the Child Care and Development Fund. In a White House press release posted close to Mother's Day, Trump touted how his administration is working to "better empower stay-at-home parents." In May, the Department of Health and Human Services issued new CCDF guidance clarifying states’ flexibility in how parents can choose among federally permitted childcare providers and services. Critics of the reported proposal, including some Republican and conservative advocates, have warned that it could increase government oversight and create new concerns involving fraud, benefit cliffs, dependency or incentives around work. Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene also labeled the idea as "socialism" in an X video, while conservative radio host Erick Erickson said on X the plan is "welfare for married people," and allegedly showed a recent pattern of the GOP pivoting toward "Diet Coke of Socialism." TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME' "I am old enough to remember a time when Republicans were against government entitlement programs," said Meghan McCain. Some conservative figures and advocates have expressed support for the concept, arguing that federal policy should provide greater support to families that choose to have a parent remain home with children. American Principles Project President Terry Schilling told Fox News Digital that the nuclear family needs to be reconsidered after years of government policies promoting multiple undergraduate and graduate degrees while delaying marriage and homeownership. "For decades, Washington paid institutions to raise kids while lonely young people delayed marriage, homeownership and children," said Schilling. "If policy helped break the family, policy can help restore it to the center of American life by putting money in parents’ hands, not in the pockets of daycare chains, unions, and nonprofits." The Advancing American Freedom (AAF) organization, founded by former Vice President Mike Pence, urged conservatives to oppose the reported plan. Rachel Greszler, AAF economist and welfare expert, told Fox News Digital in an interview that "government is not the solution to family life." "I fear that if we cross into that, that is taking what is supposed to be like a work-oriented welfare program and turning it into social engineering," she said. Greszler expressed concern that sending government checks to stay-at-home parents would inevitably require guardrails to prevent fraud and abuse — potentially bringing greater government scrutiny into the home. TRUMP’S WELFARE REFORMS ARE A MAJOR VICTORY. BUREAUCRATS COULD STILL WRECK THEM "If we are going to invite checks for parents who are staying home with their children, you are also going to be inviting the government into your home to make sure that you are doing what they think you should be doing with a stay-at-home parent check," said Greszler. She warned that even if conservatives are comfortable with how a Republican administration uses the program, establishing that government power could have unintended consequences if control of the White House changes hands. "I worry that this would open the door into using taxpayer funds for social engineering. That in a different administration after another election could be used for the exact opposite intent of what certain conservatives are looking for right now to use it," Greszler added. DRIVEN BY PROGRESSIVE DOOMISM, LIBERALS ARE HAVING FEWER BABIES THAN CONSERVATIVE FAMILIES Schilling said the earlier Americans marry and start families, the more prosperous the country will be, and this program will give support to married families over commercial daycare networks to raise children. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Traditional welfare routes money through middlemen and too often subsidized family breakdown. This proposal works on the same principle as Republican healthcare reforms: instead of sending subsidies to insurance companies, put the money directly in the hands of families," he said. Schilling says critics call it dependency when a parent stays home, but call it "investment" when a bureaucracy does it. Florida GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna shared an article on the plan and wrote, "Being a stay-at-home parent is a full-time job and there should be resources and reward available to families that do this." Fox News Digital reached out to the office of the vice president and the White House for comment.

articles.title: Congress is failing faith communities on security funding at the worst time
articles.summary: For too long, Jews and other faith-based communities have been forced to shoulder the financial and emotional burdens of protecting ourselves from hate.
articles.body:
American Jews around the country celebrated Rosh Hashanah — our New Year — last weekend and are getting ready to observe Yom Kippur — our Day of Atonement — next week. These are our “High Holy Days,” the two most sacred holidays on the Jewish calendar.

Having led one of the largest Jewish advocacy organizations in our nation’s capital region for the past 25 years, I get asked the same question every year around this time: How are you keeping the Jewish community safe?

It is an understandable and important question. The High Holy Days bring, by far, the largest attendance to our synagogues each year. We live in a time when antisemitic threats and violence have become frighteningly common, and security needs are paramount.

For too long, Jews and other faith-based communities have been forced to shoulder the financial and emotional burdens of protecting ourselves from hate. Ensuring the safety of our families and communities will always be our top priority. But we cannot do it alone, nor should we have to. It is the government’s responsibility to protect its citizens and provide us with the resources to do so.

So, the right question to ask lawmakers in Washington is what are you doing to keep us safe? Right now, the answer is nowhere near enough. Unless and until that changes, the Jewish community and many others will continue to be vulnerable targets.

Being Jewish is becoming increasingly unsafe. A recent report stated it plainly: “In both the number of lethal attacks and the number of casualties, 2025 was the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks” against Jewish communities globally in more than three decades.

Last year, the United States averaged 17 antisemitic attacks per day. Two of our brightest lights — Israeli embassy staffers Sarah Milgrim and Yaron Lischinsky — were murdered outside the Capital Jewish Museum, just steps from the U.S. Capitol. Approximately 300 other Jews were physically assaulted in incidents around the country.

The sheer volume reflects the extraordinary threats our community faces. Jews comprise a mere 2 percent of the U.S. population yet were on the receiving end of 63 percent of religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025, according to the FBI.

The need for more security support to protect our families and institutions has never been greater. Security costs for Jewish communities now amount to an astonishing $1 billion annually, with the average Jewish communal institution spending roughly $225,000 on security needs..

But something has to give. Threats are rising, costs are soaring and there’s only so much that congregations and families can do on their own.

The federal government must provide more help. In 2004, Congress established the Nonprofit Security Grant Program , which provides security grant funding for nonprofit organizations at high risk of hate crimes or terrorist attacks. As attacks increase and security costs rise, this program should be keeping pace with growing needs.

Instead, it’s the opposite . Last year, nonprofits and religious institutions requested $1.3 billion from the program, but Congress only appropriated $266 million. Of the 8,000 institutions that applied for funding, about 6,400 didn’t receive a dime.

This is unacceptable. Congress should provide sufficient funding to meet demand. Its refusal to do so is a moral failure by both parties.

Increasingly, advocates and institutions are being forced to look elsewhere for leadership. Over the past decade, my organization has led efforts to create similar nonprofit security grant programs at the state and local level in Maryland , Virginia and Washington, D.C . They help cover capital improvements like security cameras and building reinforcements, as well as operating costs like additional security guards.

They also move quickly. For example, within days of the terrorist attack on Temple Israel in Bloomfield, Michigan earlier this year, officials in Montgomery County, Maryland allocated $500,000 in emergency security funding through the county’s program to guard against copycat attacks. Any institution that had previously received funding through the program — not only synagogues, but also churches, mosques, schools and community centers — could apply. Washington D.C.’s program also came through with an additional $120,000.

The federal government should be following suit. Earlier this year, hundreds of Jewish leaders came to Washington to lobby Congress to increase funding for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program to at least $1 billion annually. Faith communities across the country need it. Indeed, that advocacy push came a day after several individuals were shot and killed at a mosque in San Diego.

But Congress continues to sit on its hands. Level funding or incremental increases are not going to cut it.

This year, Rosh Hashanah began on the evening of Sept. 11, exactly 25 years after the worst terrorist attack in American history. We gathered to remember those we lost and recommitted ourselves to doing our part to prevent future tragedies.

The question for our leaders in Washington remains: Will you finally do what you need to do?

Ron Halber is CEO of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Washington .

articles.title: Democratic senators request Pentagon provide ‘bare minimum’ on cost of Iran war
articles.summary: Nearly the entire Democratic caucus in the Senate is demanding that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with a full accounting of the cost of the war in Iran along with related budget requests, as frustration grows that the Pentagon is not being forthcoming about the war and its fiscal impact.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Nearly the entire Democratic caucus in the Senate is demanding that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide Congress with a full accounting of the cost of the Iran war along with related budget requests, as frustration grows that the Pentagon is not being forthcoming about the conflict and its fiscal impact. Forty-six Democratic senators sent a letter to Hegseth early Thursday demanding a detailed breakdown of the cost of military operations against Iran. The letter was spearheaded by Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. While the Pentagon has provided some estimates, it has not detailed the total cost of the war, including how much it would cost to repair damage to U.S. military bases, replace destroyed air and naval assets, and refurbish ships and aircraft ground down by seven months of war. The lawmakers sent the letter as they consider a Pentagon request for $67 billion in additional funding and amid deepening frustration, among Democrats and some Republicans, over the direction of the war, which appears to be in a stalemate, and the caliber of information the Pentagon is providing members of Congress. “Despite your stated needs, you have repeatedly refused to share basic information that previous administrations, Republican and Democratic, provided to the American public and Congress during times of war,” the letter states, citing the lack of Pentagon briefings for Congress or the media. Only Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, who has faced ongoing questions about leaving the Democratic Party, declined to sign the letter. Fetterman said in a statement to NBC News that his record has been consistent. “I’ve always been at odds with my fellow Democrats over how we hold Iran accountable. I’ll continue to remain an unapologetic supporter of efforts to confront the Iranian regime and its proxies,” he said. The Pentagon didn’t immediately comment. Earlier this week, NBC News reported that the Defense Department inspector general issued its first report on the war, acknowledging a munitions shortage and saying the cost of the conflict was about $33 billion, excluding the repair of damaged facilities and other costs, as of June 30. A Congressional Budget Office report, issued Tuesday, put the cost of the war at $38 billion and concluded that the conflict was driving up inflation for Americans. Critics of those estimates believe they fail to capture the true costs of the war. During a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in late July, Hegseth put the cost of the Iran war so far at $37.5 billion. He said his estimate included payroll, operation, maintenance and other “anticipated” costs through the end of the budget year. In addition to the true costs of the war, the senators also are requesting a breakdown of the Pentagon’s $67 billion supplemental budget request, as well as an accounting of money spent so far of the roughly $34 billion from the tax and spending bill President Donald Trump signed last year. In the letter, the senators lamented the lack of public briefings or hearings on the war. During the first six months of the Iraq War in 2003, then-Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld briefed Congress 20 times, and he briefed the media more than 70 times during the first month of that war, the letter says. “In stark contrast, you have briefed Congress just seven times in that same period and in those appearances, refused to answer basic questions about the objectives and cost of this war,” the letter to Hegseth says. Hegseth has briefed the Pentagon press corps eight times since the start of the Iran war in February. The last briefing was in May. During the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, the letter said, the Pentagon regularly asked for additional funding, so-called supplementals, and provided Congress with documents detailing the request that were more than 100 pages long. The Pentagon’s supplemental request for the $67 billion was seven pages and included only vague references to individual items, the letter said, citing a $1.2 billion request for “administration priorities.” To make the lawmakers’ point, the letter uses Hegseth’s own statement last year saying American taxpayers deserve to know where their money goes and how it’s spent. “We agree,” the senators write.

articles.title: Political insider turns anti-incumbent table on 8-year Dem in key Senate race: 'Hasn't delivered'
articles.summary: John E. Sununu flips the anti-incumbent script on Chris Pappas, calling him ineffective on highway funding as the NH Senate race hits toss up.
articles.body: CONCORD, N.H. - A Republican running to flip a blue Senate seat in a crucial battleground state is flipping the script on the Democrats' anti-incumbent argument. Former Sen. John E. Sununu, the GOP Senate nominee who's running to return to Capitol Hill after 18 years away, charges that his Democratic rival, Rep. Chris Pappas, has "been in Washington for 8 years and hasn't delivered for New Hampshire." Sununu and Pappas are facing off in the midterm election in the battle to succeed retiring longtime Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen in a race that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if Republicans hold their control of the Senate. "He has attempted very little in Congress. He's accomplished even less," Sununu said in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview this week, as he blasted Pappas, a four-term congressman. THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DETERMINE IF REPUBLICANS HOLD THE SENATE Sununu was interviewed ahead of a move by the Cook Political Report, a top nonpartisan campaign handicapper, to shift the race in New Hampshire from lean Democrat to toss-up. Earlier this month, another leading nonpartisan handicapper, Inside Elections, also changed their rating to a toss-up. It was a rare move in favor of the Republicans amid a political cycle where the GOP is facing traditional political headwinds for the party in power in D.C.. Republicans are also confronting an extremely rough political climate fueled by persistent inflation, soaring fuel prices due to the ongoing war with Iran, and President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings. So what's Sununu's secret sauce? Part of it is his last name, which is a political brand in New Hampshire. Sununu's father, John E. Sununu, served six years as governor before heading to Washington, D.C., as then-President George H.W. Bush's White House chief of staff. And one of his younger brothers, Chris Sununu, recently served eight years as governor before taking a break from politics. But also boosting Sununu, his strategy to blast Pappas as a do-nothing member of Congress during another anti-incumbent election cycle, which is a turn of the tables on the Democrats' playbook. CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE BATTLE FOR THE SENATE "He's been on the Transportation Committee for eight years, and New Hampshire is dead last in highway funding in New England. That hurts New Hampshire. His ineffectiveness is doing damage to the state because we're not getting the support we need from Washington," Sununu claimed. While it doesn't rank dead last in every single metric or category, New Hampshire receives some of the lowest total and per-capita levels of federal funding for roads, highways and bridges of any state in the country, according to federal and state figures. Pappas, earlier this year, introduced the Highway Fair Share Act, a bill to increase federal funding for infrastructure and transportation projects for New Hampshire by requiring that each state receive at least 0.5% of the total federal-aid highway formula funding. Pappas and the rest of the all-Democratic congressional delegation in June highlighted $9 million in federal funding for New Hampshire projects. "Chris Pappas has led efforts to expand healthcare benefits for 3.5 million veterans, bring high-speed internet to towns across New Hampshire, put more money back in the pockets of working parents, and secure millions of dollars to improve and repair roads, bridges, and buildings," Pappas Campaign Manager Rachel Petri told Fox News Digital, as she shared a long list of funding accomplishments by the congressman. Petri said, "Chris is rated among the most effective and bipartisan lawmakers and his record stands in stark contrast to John Sununu’s record of voting to cut Medicare, leading efforts to privatize Social Security, and backing Donald Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran." Sununu's anti-incumbent argument is a bit ironic, considering he spent six years in the House and a term in the Senate before losing a rematch with then-former Gov. Shaheen in the 2008 election. Looking back at his years on Capitol Hill, Sununu touted his record "of writing and passing legislation under Democrat presidents, Republican presidents, a Democrat Congress, Republican Congress." But he also emphasized, "I've been in the private sector for the last 16 years. That's a good thing, working for tech firms and small businesses, the Waterville Valley ski area [the Sununu family has had a controlling interest in the resort since 2010], teaching college. It's... a perspective that I think is missing from Washington." WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLLS IN KEY MIDTERM RACES SHOW Pappas, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, highlighted that New Hampshire is "a state of voters who are pragmatic, who want their lives to be better and want problems to be solved, and I can demonstrate the ways that I've been working on those issues." "It's expanding access to health care, building more affordable housing in New Hampshire, and ensuring that we're standing up to an administration that's ignoring the day-to-day concerns of Granite Staters," he added. But Sununu wasn't the only one taking aim at Pappas as a do-nothing incumbent. Even his long-shot socialist rival in last week's primary took a shot. First-time candidate and scientist Karishma Manzur, in a recent Fox News Digital interview, charged that "all [Pappas] wants to do is just get his little cushy job and go to D.C., go to all these parties and these restaurants and just do whatever the bare minimum is." Pappas ended up crushing Manzur in the primary by a two-to-one margin, and Sununu defeated former Sen. Scott Brown in a landslide to capture the GOP nomination. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER With the general election sprint underway, Republican-aligned outside groups are now pouring millions into the state to target Pappas. And Pappas is using this week's Cook Political Report race rating to ring an alarm. "MAGA super PACs are pouring millions of dollars a week into New Hampshire to try to flip this seat. And this race is officially a Toss Up," he warned on social media. And Pappas told Fox News Digital recently that Sununu is "backed up by out-of-state special interests and dark money in this campaign. They're outspending us 3 to 1 on TV." Firing back, this week a Democrat-aligned super PAC started running ads charging that, after he left the Senate, Sununu cashed in by working for lobbying firms. Sununu was endorsed earlier this year by Trump, and since then Democrats have repeatedly tied the president, whose approval ratings are well into negative territory in New Hampshire, to Sununu. Pappas called Sununu Trump's "hand-picked candidate." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Asked about the full-court press by Pappas and Democrats to anchor him to Trump, Sununu told Fox News Digital, "I've never even met the president." But contrasting himself with Pappas, Sununu added that "there's no question I'll be a much more effective voice with this administration."

articles.title: Federal judge ties ICE agents' hands with ruling on warrantless Southern California arrests
articles.summary: A federal judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking ICE from carrying out warrantless immigration arrests unless the target is likely to escape before a warrant is obtained.
articles.body: A federal judge with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California issued a preliminary injunction to block the U.S. government from conducting warrantless civil immigration arrests in the district unless the arrestee is deemed likely to escape before a warrant can be procured. "Defendants are enjoined from enforcing their policy and practice of making warrantless civil immigration arrests in this District without a prearrest individualized determination by the arresting agent or officer of probable cause that the person being arrested is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, as required by 8 U.S.C. 1357(a)(2) and 8 C.F.R. § 287.8(c)(2)," the order signed by U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong reads, in part. Frimpong was nominated by former President Joe Biden during his White House tenure. EXCLUSIVE: 25 YEARS AFTER 9/11, ICE SAYS MORE THAN 2K KNOWN OR SUSPECTED TERRORISTS HAVE BEEN DEPORTED "Mere presence within the United States in violation of United States immigration law is not, by itself, sufficient to conclude that a person is likely to escape before a warrant for arrest can be obtained," the judge's order notes. The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California encompasses the following counties: Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties. articles.title: Trump’s $5K checks could join stack of past unfulfilled promises, former Congress budget chief warns
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 tariff checks and DOGE savings promises are unlikely to arrive, says former CBO Director Douglas Holz-Eakin.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's latest cash promise to Americans is unlikely to come to fruition, just like others before it, an economist and former congressional budget hawk told Fox News Digital. "So the president has promised a lot of checks, the most recent being $5,000 to every American if Republicans hold on to the House and Senate. We ever going to see these? Well, I don't think so," said Douglas Holz-Eakin, president of fiscal policy think tank American Action Forum. Holz-Eakin previously served as the director of the Congressional Budget Office and as the director of domestic and economic policy for late Republican Sen. John McCain's 2008 presidential campaign. TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' "The DOGE checks were never realistic because DOGE was never going to save that much money," said Holz-Eakin in reference to the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency's sweeping layoffs and budget cuts to federal agencies. He continued: "And the tariff checks were never that realistic because [Trump] didn't have the authority to issue the checks, and that's actually true of all of these promises." Holz-Eakin also mentioned the Trump administration's recently proposed plan to give $9,000 checks to stay-at-home mothers likely won't come through either. "Trying to get money to stay at home moms for childcare, there's a route to that, but it's gonna be tough ... we'll see if they actually pull it off," he said. "So, I would be skeptical that any of these checks are gonna be in your mailbox very soon." The internationally-known economist likened the Trump administration's fiscal policy to that of former President Joe Biden's Democratic administration. "I think we've seen two successive administrations get themselves in the following position: inflation is too high and wages aren't keeping up with it. Well, that's failing at the American dream," Holz-Eakin explained. THE FED JUST THREW A WRENCH IN TRUMP'S MIDTERM ECONOMIC MESSAGE He said that getting inflation under control was the first step in restoring order, as well as being "utterly supportive" of the Federal Reserve, which Holz-Eakin says is working to achieve that goal. The Fed hiked interest rates Wednesday for the first time in three years, and signaled that more rate increases could be coming. This comes despite Trump's push to have the world's most powerful central bank lower interest rates to lessen the monthly burden on Americans seeking home and auto loans. "Inflation remains elevated," the Federal Open Market Committee said in a post-meeting statement. "Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability." "You need to have, I think, a more vibrant economy, and this economy is doing okay, but it's putting up with a lot of headwinds," said Holz-Eakin. He named specific Trump administration policy decisions he says are to blame for the lackluster economy, which has burdened the middle class as grocery prices continue to rise. "The first headwinds were tariffs, second headwinds were the oil prices and fight with Iran, and we need to get past those battles, and let the economy just go, and ... that would be a better environment for the families," he told Fox News Digital. CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100 As for overall fiscal policy, Holz-Eakin says he's worried that the country is going in the wrong direction when it comes to economic and fiscal policy. "I'm a former director of the Congressional Budget Office. I have to every day get up and look at the books and wonder, 'how's this going to add up?'" he said. "And right now it doesn't add up." "We're $41 trillion in debt. The deficit is $2 trillion every year and it's getting larger. You can't just keep putting people on the on government programs. It won't add up." "I'd like to see a bit of a U-turn that got the debt under control, didn't spend quite so much money, and got through this without having to raise our taxes. So, that sounds like an old-school conservative plan to me, but that's not what we're seeing right now." Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Trump's economic promises, but did not hear back at time of publication.

articles.title: Powerful teachers' unions share striking link with states struggling to teach kids to read
articles.summary: A Progressive Policy Institute study links strong teachers unions to weaker student literacy, with eight of the 10 lowest-scoring states affected.
articles.body: States with stronger teachers' unions tend to have weaker literacy performance and have adopted fewer of the policies credited with improving reading outcomes, according to a new analysis from a center-left think tank. Eight of the 10 states to score among the worst in the Progressive Policy Institute’s (PPI) assessment of early-literacy policies were home to powerful teachers' unions. Among the top 60% of states in terms of early-literacy policy scores, only four had strong teachers' unions. Mississippi, Arkansas, Georgia, Louisiana, South Carolina and Indiana, all Republican-leaning states with weak unions, were among the states with the best literacy outcomes. Maine, New York, Illinois, Hawaii, Washington and Rhode Island, blue states, were among the worst. ARKANSAS STUDENTS OUTPERFORM NATIONAL AVERAGE AFTER UNIVERSAL SCHOOL CHOICE EXPANSION, GOVERNOR SAYS The pattern isn't universal. Maryland, a blue state with a strong teachers' union, has posted strong reading results, while South Dakota, a red state with a weaker union, has struggled. The differences suggest union strength and party control alone don't explain states' reading performance. Rachel Canter, PPI’s director of education policy, conducted the analysis with colleagues by comparing teacher-union strength rankings with states’ early-literacy policy scores. Canter is also one of the people behind the slate of educational reforms in Mississippi that propelled the state from among the worst in the country for educational outcomes to among the best. "Democrats, however, don’t often ask me how to replicate Mississippi’s success," Canter said. "They ask if it’s possible at all, given the power of teachers’ unions in their home states." Teachers' unions, according to Canter, exert massive amounts of influence over both educational policies and how those policies are implemented in the classroom. This can make schools in states with stronger unions slower to adapt to challenges or to adopt new, better methods. TEACHERS UNION FACING YEARS OF DEFICITS SEEKS TO BECOME OREGON'S LARGEST PAC, INTERNAL DOCUMENTS SHOW Mississippi’s reforms, among other things, added kindergarten-through-third-grade screenings, literacy coaches, individual reading plans and held back third-graders who failed the state reading test. The state reinforced those measures with science-based reading instruction, increased teacher training and tougher licensing requirements. Tweaks to teaching like these can be difficult to achieve in states with influential teachers' unions, with labor reps arguing that the changes place undue burdens on educators. ILLINOIS DEMOCRATIC GOVERNOR BUCKS TEACHERS' UNIONS IN SUPPORT FOR STATEWIDE CLASSROOM PHONE BAN Many of the states that underperformed in the Progressive Policy Institute’s study also have Democratic leadership. Teachers’ unions spend hundreds of millions of dollars every electoral cycle on electing Democrats and pushing left-of-center policies. "States dominated by Democrats have been slower to embrace similar reforms," Canter said. "Organized labor might explain some of this gap." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Multiple GOP-led Southern states have adopted educational reforms similar to those introduced in Mississippi. Those same states dominated the Progressive Policy Institute’s rankings of the states with the best student literacy.

articles.title: Historic newspaper gives El-Sayed a savage rebuke for hiding his past while endorsing his opponent
articles.summary: The Detroit News endorsed Mike Rogers for Michigan's Senate race while blasting Abdul El-Sayed for deleting thousands of past social media posts.
articles.body: A top newspaper in battleground Michigan is skewering left-wing Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed over past radical rhetoric as it endorses Republican rival former Rep. Mike Rogers in a crucial midterm showdown. The race between El-Sayed and Rogers to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is a must-win battle for the Democrats as they try to recapture the Senate majority from the GOP. The Detroit News, which has the second-largest newspaper circulation in Michigan, charged in its endorsement of Rogers that El-Sayed "has worked so hard covering his tracks leading up to this Senate race that it's impossible to know who he really is or where he would stand in the Senate." WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POLLING "He has deleted social media posts that reportedly called into question his attitude about America in the aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. He's taken down roughly 100 YouTube videos that paint an unflattering picture of him and his cultural views," the conservative-leaning newspaper argued. "A candidate who feels the need to hide his past from voters is not someone who can be trusted to be the same person after Election Day as he was on the campaign trail." As he runs for the Senate, El-Sayed has removed or archived thousands of past social media posts and older podcast/YouTube videos. Some of those past comments include floating the idea of abandoning fireworks on July 4th, suggesting replacing the nation's Second Amendment with the "right to have health care," and one-time support for the "defund the police" movement. El-Sayed, who was captain of his high school football team, also criticized football's ties to toxic masculinity and a "bro culture." DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The Rogers campaign and other Republicans have blasted El-Sayed for many of his past controversial comments. The El-Sayed campaign said this summer that some of the past comments were removed "to prevent any old posts from being taken out of context." And last week, around the 9/11 25th anniversary, the El-Sayed campaign emphasized that "Abdul has always unequivocally condemned terrorism and the September 11 attacks." Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for additional comment on the Detroit News' criticisms, but didn't receive a response at the time this story was published. The newspaper praised Rogers, calling him "the prototype of a United States Senator." The 63-year-old Republican left Congress at the end of 2014, having been elected to his House seat seven times by his mid-Michigan constituents. Rogers then embarked on a successful career in private industry, becoming an expert in cybersecurity," the newspaper noted as it referred to his career. articles.title: Fraud mastermind behind multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme that victimized Travis Kelce is illegal immigrant
articles.summary: Siddharth Jawahar, an illegal immigrant from India, was sentenced to 11 years for a $35 million Ponzi scheme that victimized Travis Kelce and NBA stars.
articles.body: The mastermind behind the multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme that even victimized NFL star Travis Kelce is an illegal immigrant from India. Thirty-eight-year-old Siddharth Jawahar was sentenced to 11 years in prison this week for running a $35 million investment wire fraud scheme. At his sentencing, Judge Zachary Bluestone said that through his investment company, Swiftarc Capital LLC, Jawahar "weaponized" investors' trust, resulting in "massive" losses for the victims. Jawahar raised more than $35 million from investors between 2016 and 2023 and only invested roughly $10 million of that total. He spent the remainder funding personal luxuries, including private jet charters, upscale apartments in Austin and New York, high-end dining, shopping sprees at clothing stores and exclusive private club memberships. He has now been ordered to pay $31.35 million in restitution to his victims. But that is not the end of Jawahar’s legal issues. He may also be subject to deportation. According to the Department of Justice and a court document reviewed by Fox News Digital, Jawahar is an illegal immigrant from India who has been living in the U.S. since 2005. TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS Further, the DOJ said that after his indictment on three counts of wire fraud and one count of investment-adviser fraud in 2023, Jawahar tried to obstruct justice by coaching a victim into giving a favorable statement to the FBI while lying about his immigration status and finances. He also tried to get his sister to remotely wipe his iPhone to hide evidence, the DOJ said. Jawahar pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in January 2026. Among Jawahar’s victims was Kelce, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end who recently married pop superstar Taylor Swift, and several NBA players, including Gary Harris, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Mason Plumlee. The DOJ said Jawahar’s victims resided in Missouri and elsewhere. FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME Instead of managing a diversified portfolio for his investors, Jawahar allocated roughly 99% of client capital into a single stock, Philip Morris Pakistan. As that position tanked, Jawahar hid the losses, issued falsified statements and used funds from new investors to pay out earlier clients. Jawahar also managed 17 additional entities that he utilized during his scheme. articles.title: Former GOP whip, Arizona Sen Jon Kyl dead at 84
articles.summary: Former Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl, an Arizona Republican who served nearly three decades in Congress, has died at age 84 following a battle with dementia.
articles.body: Former Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl, R-Ariz., is dead at the age of 84, his family announced Thursday. Kyl was first sworn in to the Senate in 1995, retiring in 2013. He briefly returned to the Senate in 2018 after former Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., died. Kyl announced he was stepping away from public life in December 2025 after receiving a diagnosis of a neurological disease that resulted in his development of dementia. Before his election to the Senate, Kyl was a member of the U.S. House of Representatives from 1987 to 1995. AN EMPTY US CAPITOL AFTER MCCAIN’S DEATH IS SOBERING REMINDER THAT THE CLOCK IS TICKING Former Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who appointed Kyl to fill McCain's seat in 2018, paid his respects to the former senator in a Thursday post on X. "Jon Kyl gave Arizona nearly three decades of principled, thoughtful leadership — and he gave me something just as valuable: his mentorship and friendship. I'll miss him deeply. Rest in peace, Senator Kyl," Ducey posted. Former Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Ariz., who served in the Senate with Kyl, also paid homage to the late lawmaker. "Arizona has lost a giant. Jon Kyl was one of the most diligent and effective public servants Arizona has ever had. I was honored to follow him in the U.S. Senate, where his example of seriousness, integrity and devotion to public service was known to all. Cheryl and I send our deepest condolences to Caryll and the entire Kyl family," Flake posted on X. Flake also gave remarks to reporters at the Capitol on Thursday. "I admired him from the get-go, when he was back in the House, and I was in Arizona. When I ran for office, he gave me the best advice I ever got. He said that, when you get back to Washington, make sure your family is aware of what you're doing, is involved in it. He said they will either resent it or revel in it. And that was the best advice I got, because we tried to follow that. And he was just… in addition to being an extremely effective public servant, he was a good man. And I think that that shined through," Flake told reporters. TILLIS' RETIREMENT ANNOUNCEMENT DRAWS REACTIONS FROM TRUMP CRITIC JEFF FLAKE, BERNIE SANDERS: 'A CULT' "For Arizona, you know, every Western state has similar issues; water issues, public land issues. And Jon took that on," Flake said. "That's the workhorse in him. I think he did nine Indian water settlements during his time, which has allowed the Indian tribes in Arizona to have the water they need and also for the state to grow sustainably," Flake continued. "And then also, in terms of his legal mind and his, you know, concern about the Supreme Court. And he was asked after he had left Congress to sherpa certain nominees through, and he was extremely effective in that because he had the respect of his colleagues." Flake also revealed that he last spoke with Kyl just before the late senator announced his dementia diagnosis. "December of last year he put out a statement. I had talked to him just before that. And it was a wonderful conversation. He was very much aware of all that the state had gone through, and I made sure to tell him how appreciative all Arizonans are of what he did for the state and what he did for the country. And, he was so devoted to his wife, Carol, and his family, and the state of Arizona," Flake said. Flake also commented on the unique situation that arose when Kyl was appointed to replace McCain. "When Senator McCain passed away, there was an appointment, and he served out that term for the last few months. So I got to serve with him in the Senate and also jokingly be the senior senator to him, which I didn't deserve. But it was just a wonderful relationship throughout," Flake said. articles.title: Scandal rocks Utah campus as student who celebrated Charlie Kirk’s death sparks online firestorm
articles.summary: A viral photo of a "Happy Kirkiversary" cake sparked a University of Utah probe into two College Republicans accused of doxxing a fellow student.
articles.body: A college student photographed with a cake mocking Charlie Kirk's death is at the center of a campus controversy that has prompted the University of Utah to investigate two College Republicans for charges of misconduct after one posted the photo online. On Sept. 10, 2026, the one-year anniversary of the conservative activist's public murder, a woman approached a group of College Republicans at an event on the school's campus and presented them with a cake. The words "Happy Kirkiversary" were written in red icing on the white cake. Students Riley Beesley, the chairman of the school's College Republicans chapter, and Rylie Barnes, also a member of the group, took exception to the stunt on a campus less than an hour's drive from another college campus where Kirk was assassinated last year. Barnes posted a photo of the cake to her X account, and it quickly went viral and led to an anonymous X user identifying the student as Sara Larsen. UNIVERSITY OF TENNESSEE CONDEMNS FLYERS APPEARING TO CELEBRATE CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION The school's College Democrats responded by saying Republicans are "waging a campaign of hate" against them. On Tuesday, the university sent emails to Beesley and Barnes requesting closed-door meetings Wednesday morning with its Student Rights and Responsibilities office. "We received information that, if accurate, may go against this priority and the policy on Student Rights and Responsibilities, and I would like to meet and hear your perspective," says a copy of one of the emails, obtained by Fox News Digital. "The report is regarding an incident that happened on or about September 11, 2026 and allegedly involves you attempting to doxx another University of Utah student over a political issue." The email was sent by the office's assistant director, Jose Morales Diaz. "Doxxing" is the act of publicly revealing, usually online, the personal information of another person, typically with the intent of causing harm to that individual. "We will talk about the information our office received, and you will have an opportunity to give your perspective of the incident if you wish. We will also talk about possible next steps, such as resolutions and educational or restorative measures if appropriate," the email said. 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS The emails also prohibited the students from recording the meetings. But shortly before the meetings were scheduled to take place, the university abruptly canceled them, according to Beesley. Diaz did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. "We found it distasteful, vile, and disgusting. Parents, alumni, students and donors deserve to know about the radical political ideologies festering on college campuses in Utah," Beesley told Fox News Digital of the cake incident. "Given today's political climate, mocking or expressing support such as this should be taken incredibly seriously and the public sphere has a right to know about the lack of morality being observed among young Democrats and those on the left." He strongly condemned doxxing, and said his group had nothing to do with the release of Larsen's information. He also condemned political violence. "We're observing patterns where those on the left find it comical to make threats, have normalized silencing opposing political viewpoints, and avoid accountability or consequences for glorifying murder," he said. "This must end." CARNEGIE MELLON 'DEEPLY CONCERNED' BY PROFESSOR'S 'HOSTILE AND THREATENING POSTS' ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH The university told Fox News Digital it can't comment on student disciplinary action, citing federal law. But Wednesday night, the school released a statement about the ongoing controversy, which has been going viral online for days and has become a national news story. "In recent days, a dispute between political groups on the University of Utah campus has resulted in allegations of harassment, threats, and the inappropriate sharing or amplification of personal information. The University of Utah is reviewing these accusations consistent with established policies, due process and applicable law," the statement said. "As we conduct this review, the university will continue to simultaneously protect freedom of expression and the safety of our students. Calls to harm someone, including electronic harassment and inappropriate sharing of information, are not protected by free speech," it continued. The school also urged the College Democrats and College Republicans groups on campus to convene with leadership in an attempt to better understand one another. It also condemned violence. COLORADO TPUSA CHAPTER ENROLLMENT 'FLAT' AFTER ELDERLY SUPPORTER WAS STRICKEN BY STUDENT WITH TACO BELL CUP Beesley was subject to an alleged violent threat on campus earlier this year, when a person threatened to "Kirk" him. "It was January 12, we were outside tabling and engaging in debates in a format similar to those organized by, let's say, Turning Point USA," Beesley told Fox News Digital at the time. "And soon after [he] declared to us, 'you should die,' followed by, 'I am going to Kirk you,' which you could only think that means I'm either using your imagination going to shoot you or kill you." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Dean Stewart, then 21, was arrested following the incident. Criminal proceedings against him are ongoing, Beesley said. An X account with the name Sara Larsen made a post on Sept. 11, 2026, apologizing for the cake stunt. Fox News Digital could not independently verify whether the account owner is the student embroiled in the controversy. "Upon reflection, it was wrong for me to celebrate, or perpetuate the celebration of, Charlie Kirk’s death. I apologize for doing so sincerely. Nobody should be murdered or persecuted for their speech," reads the tweet — the only post present on an account with 311 followers that was created in February 2017.

articles.title: AI hysteria has a Y2K problem — and the stakes this time could be far higher
articles.summary: Critics compare AI regulation fears to Y2K and climate change hysteria, arguing the tech industry can self-correct without sweeping government action.
articles.body: Washington’s growing alarm over artificial intelligence is beginning to echo Y2K, experts say, when dire warnings of technological catastrophe prompted a massive scramble to avert failures that ultimately proved far less severe than feared. "You could draw all sorts of scary scenarios with Y2K as well. The financial system was just going to collapse because people had not written their programs for the year 2000. I had been writing programs in the 1980s for the government, so I'm well aware of the program," Junk Science publisher and founder Steven Milloy told Fox News Digital. "But of course, the tech industry knew about the problem, and to the extent that was a real problem, took action to fix it. The same can happen with AI," Milloy added. RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Y2K was a computer bug that raised fears systems could fail when the calendar changed from 1999 to 2000. The U.S. spent an estimated $100 billion, $200 billion adjusted for today's inflation, in preparing for the problem, according to a 2000 Senate report. When the new millennium arrived, there were few major disruptions. President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and Democrats cry foul before midterm elections. DEMOCRATS EMBRACED AI’S GROWTH BEFORE TRUMP CAME ALONG — NOW THEY WANT TO SLOW IT DOWN "Democrats are capitalizing on the fears of Americans that angst over AI," Heritage Foundation technology analyst Annie Chestnut Tutor told Fox News Digital. Democrats are increasingly calling for government guardrails on AI, citing potential threats ranging from job losses and inequality to risks to democracy and humanity. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, for instance, wrote in April that AI "kills jobs, equality, connection, democracy and maybe the human race." But the apocalyptic warnings are not coming only from Washington. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company over concerns about the race toward self-improving AI, warning that its developers are "gambling with our lives" and that such systems could potentially "kill us all by the end of the decade." SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE Y2K sparked similar fears, as warnings spread of potential power-grid failures, disruptions to air travel and air-traffic control, and even predictions that planes could fall from the sky. The Trump administration has backed targeted safeguards, including AI-powered cyber defenses for critical infrastructure, criminal enforcement against AI-enabled hacking and proposed measures to limit AI-driven child exploitation. Tutor offered a nuanced Y2K comparison, arguing that the episode showed how technological risks can be addressed before they become potentially catastrophic. "The reason now, like, we all laugh about Y2K is because actually software engineers and, like, financial analysts, they've worked really hard to ensure that the catastrophic incidents [didn’t] happen," Tutor said. AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK "I think the same thing could happen with AI," she added. "If AI is built right, it can be more beneficial to Americans than the doomsday scenario." Milloy said the Y2K comparison also fits a pattern he sees with climate change, with dire warnings of an existential threat followed by calls for sweeping government intervention. Climate warnings have likewise been framed in apocalyptic terms, including predictions that entire nations could be wiped out by global warming, Arctic summer ice could disappear within years and Glacier National Park’s glaciers would vanish by 2020. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION "There are a lot of parallels between climate hysteria and AI hysteria," Milloy said. "Climate was existential. It was going to destroy the planet, and by implication, humanity. As we learned last week, AI is going to destroy humanity also on a very short time frame." Milloy argued that while lawmakers are crying foul, they have not established enough specific evidence of catastrophic AI scenarios to justify sweeping restrictions. Trump has responded to AI warnings by calling them a "hoax," reviving the language he has used for years to dismiss climate change concerns. "Give me a real-life practical scenario of how this can happen," he said. "And then if you know what the scenario is, then you can stop it." DAVID MARCUS: BIG TECH INVENTED AI DOOMSDAY TO DUCK REAL LIFE PROBLEMS SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Milloy warned that overly broad regulation could carry its own cost by slowing technological advances before their benefits are fully understood. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The opportunity costs are potentially huge," Milloy said, pointing to potential AI-assisted advances in medicine and productivity while acknowledging that their ultimate scale remains unknown.

articles.title: Jon Kyl, ‘workhorse’ former U.S. senator of Arizona, dies at 84
articles.summary: Former U.S.Senator Jon Kyl, Republican of Arizona, dies at 84. He guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
articles.body: PHOENIX — Former U.S. Sen. Jon Kyl, a longtime Republican lawmaker from Arizona who shaped landmark water policies in the U.S. West and guided the confirmation of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, has died. He was 84. Kyl died Wednesday night from a neurological disorder, said Gordon James, a communications professional who is longtime friends with the Kyl family. Kyl had withdrawn from public life in December 2025 after announcing he had been diagnosed with dementia. Kyl spent almost three decades in Congress, serving in both chambers, and watched his party undergo a drastic transformation, with his career spanning Ronald Reagan’s presidency to President Donald Trump’s first term. Former Republican Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey, who considered Kyl a mentor, described the former senator in a February 2025 interview with The Associated Press as a true statesman and a “workhorse” among Washington, D.C.’s “showhorses.” “If you saw him on the plane, he was sitting in the aisle, in coach, and he was reading,” Ducey said. “And he was reading potential bills or Senate business.” Kyl rose to a leadership position during his last full term in the Senate, when his Republican colleagues selected him as minority whip. After retiring from politics in 2013 and becoming a lobbyist, Kyl returned to Congress briefly in 2018, when Ducey appointed him to fill the vacancy left by the late U.S. Sen. John McCain. His appointment drew high praise from Trump, who said he was looking forward to working with “the extraordinary senator.” Kyl stayed for less than four months before rejoining lobbying firm Covington and Burling. “At the federal level, and I regret to say that this is the case, but probably a lot of my better achievements were in preventing bad things from happening (rather) than forcing good things to happen,” Kyl said in a 2012 conversation with former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor. Kyl was born in Oakland, Nebraska, on April 25, 1942, and grew up in a rural farming district in Iowa that his father represented in the U.S. House. At 18, he headed southwest to attend the University of Arizona, where he met his wife, Caryll, and earned a law degree. Before being elected for the first of his four terms in the House in 1987, Kyl was a key participant in shaping Arizona’s 1980 groundwater code as a lawyer representing a large water utility. The first-of-its-kind code created a regulatory framework for managing groundwater in the drought-stricken state, largely centering on the state’s population centers, including Phoenix and Tucson. In 2004, Kyl authored legislation that provided one of the largest tribal water rights settlements, which, after a decades-long battle, gave the Gila River Indian Community enough water to fill nearly 313,500 Olympic-sized swimming pools annually. Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, who later served as majority leader, called Kyl’s work ethic “legendary” in a 2012 floor speech and said Kyl had labored mostly behind the scenes for 15 years to advance the settlement. “It was one of the hardest things I’ve ever done, but I was in a position to be the catalyst,” Kyl told the Phoenix New Times in a 2006 interview. “There wasn’t anybody else who could do that water deal. And it had to be done.” Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy takes its name from him. Its director, Sarah Porter, said Kyl was generous with his time and an effective member of the state’s congressional delegation who took a practical approach to water policy. “He’s always sort of cared about the public good and been able to think about, ‘What will this mean for the generations to come?’” Porter said, adding that Kyl remained “quite a dynamo” until recent years, as his wife battled health problems. Ducey said Kyl was a “giant” in the Senate, further describing him as serious, engaging, forthright and thoughtful. His biggest impacts, Ducey said, came from the way he kept the Republican caucus together in opposition to Obamacare and his staunch support of Israel. Kyl also backed legislation to authorize construction of a fence stretching hundreds of miles along the U.S.-Mexico border. He later joined with Democrats to support a bill that would provide a path to citizenship and temporary guest-worker status for those in the U.S. without authorization. The proposal ultimately failed. As a lobbyist, Kyl helped guide the confirmation of Trump-picked U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. When Kyl returned to the halls of Congress in 2018, he was known as Kavanaugh’s chief Sherpa — an informal but widely known term for a nominee’s guide to the political tundra in the Senate. In a statement disclosing his dementia diagnosis, Kyl harkened back to the words of Reagan, when the former president revealed his own Alzheimer’s diagnosis and said he was starting a journey that would lead him to the end of his life. Kyl said he shared Reagan’s confidence for Arizona and the nation’s future, and that despite his diagnosis, he was a “very fortunate man.”

articles.title: Wife of US scholar jailed in China asks Trump raise arrest at Xi meeting
articles.summary: Sylvia Zin is among the family members of people imprisoned in China who are seeking Trump's help when he hosts the country's leader next week.
articles.body:
The wife of a US scholar imprisoned in China on charges of spying and endangering national security has asked President Donald Trump to secure his release when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House next week.

U Min Zin, the director at a think tank focused on Myanmar, was arrested on 3 June after travelling to the Chinese city of Kunming for an academic conference.

"I'm deeply hopeful that President Trump will raise my husband's case with President Xi Jinping at the summit next week," his wife, Sylvia Zin, testified to Congress on Wednesday.

Xi is due to arrive for a state visit to Washington DC on Wednesday. It comes after Xi hosted Trump for a visit to Beijing in May.

Ahead of the meeting, families of prisoners being held in China have travelled to the US capital to advocate for their release.

Sylvia Zin appeared before the House Foreign Affairs Committee East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee on Wednesday for a hearing titled Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea's Repression.

In her remarks, Zin said she believed Trump would also be able to secure the release of Chen Youlin, a US seismologist who tracks nuclear tests that has been held in prison in China for two years.

"Knowing the president's historic record on bringing wrongfully detained Americans home has reassured me that he will also be able to secure the swift release of Min Zin and other wrongfully detained citizens," she said.

Congresswoman Young Kim, the chairwoman of the subcommittee, opened the hearing by warning Americans: "If you travel to China, Beijing may take you hostage as leverage in diplomatic negotiation."

Speaking about Zin's arrest, she added: "Beijing wanted to send a message to those whose research inconvenienced it, and detained Mr Zin ahead of the upcoming Trump-Xi summit."

Min Zin, a student activist during Myanmar's 1988 pro-democracy movement, directs the Myanmar Institute for Strategic and Policy Studies (ISP-Myanmar), a think tank that studies China's role in Myanmar, including Chinese interests, relations, and regional influence.

The son of Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai also appeared on Capitol Hill to call on Trump to secure his father's release. The US president previously raised the case with Xi, telling reporters that his Chinese counterpart "told me that would be a tough one".

Asked for comment on Thursday, a senior White House official, speaking anonymously, told the BBC: "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the President."

China arrests US scholar suspected of spying

Last month, the US State Department said that two Americans - U Min Zin and Chen Youlin - were being "wrongfully detained" in China.

This designation in the US allows the cases to be transferred to the office of the Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs - raising the profile of each case and allowing the US government to allocate more resources to securing their release.

Zin, who lives in Thailand, told the committee on Wednesday that she has not yet been able to speak to her husband in jail, "so every month, we anxiously await his consular visits because they reassure us that he is alive".

Zin said US officials had told her that Min Zin was being subjected to up to six hours of interrogations each day when he first arrived in jail.

"I'm trying to be strong for our daughter, but I'm constantly wondering if he's OK and how to get him back home to us," she said.

Last time Trump and Xi formally met, Trump pressed for the return of another American in jail. Underground church leader Jin Mingri was freed two months after Trump's request.

articles.title: Unearthed audio exposes stunning El-Sayed admission about his healthcare pitch
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's 2011 comments reveal his long-standing vision for Medicare-for-all and making healthcare more expensive for wealthier patients.
articles.body: Over a decade before becoming the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed acknowledged that his vision for healthcare would require different costs for patients depending on wealth status. "We’re actually just going to give other people access to what you have and make yours more expensive. We’re not asking you to lose access. We’re just making yours more expensive. And not that much so, in fact. We’re making it marginally more expensive," El-Sayed said in a 2011 appearance on the "Sense and Sustainability" podcast. His resurfaced comments, made as part of a program on inequalities in healthcare, reveal El-Sayed’s long-standing thinking behind his proposed policy changes. DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE Fifteen years later, El-Sayed has made an expansion of healthcare in the U.S. a key part of his platform as he wages a bid to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich. In particular, he has championed Medicare-for-all, an expansion of the federal program that covers healthcare costs for U.S. citizens over the age of 65 and for some younger recipients with long-term disabilities. El-Sayed’s plan would expand public coverage for everyone, regardless of income, age or job. "Medicare-for-all means no premium, no co-pay, no deductible. Doesn’t matter if you get a job, lose a job, turn 26, turn 65, get married, get divorced — it is there for you," El-Sayed said in a post to X earlier this year. Skeptics of the plan argue it is too expensive and does little to address existing inefficiencies in the American healthcare system. In 2019, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., took to the Senate floor to blast the idea, calling it a straitjacket solution that would undermine health care quality. LIZ PEEK: MICHIGAN CAN STOP THE SOCIALIST FEVER RAGE — OR WATCH IT SWALLOW THE SENATE "The [Congressional Budget Office] projects in its report on a single-payer plan that government spending on health care would increase substantially. They go on to say to cover the massive cost of government-run care, income taxes would have to at least double. Income taxes, American families — at least double," Barrasso said. "Mark my words, Medicare-for-all would soon become Medicare for none." Despite its hefty price tag, in El-Sayed’s view, the plan is key to ensuring equality of outcomes, even if individual patients are charged differently. He expounded on his design in the 2011 interview. "We wouldn’t necessarily be ‘stealing from the rich to give to the poor’ in the U.S. because the rich will always have the ability to pay for the care that they need," El-Sayed said. "The argument would be that everyone’s premiums would go up a little bit. But for the people who actually have premiums now, what they’re losing in terms of the added costs on their health plans are more manageable to them than is the absolute lack of access to healthcare among the people that don’t have it now." El-Sayed argued that his vision would make costs only marginally more expensive for top earners. Having cleared the Democratic primary in Michigan, El-Sayed will face Republican challenger Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in the state's Nov. 3 general election.

articles.title: Mamdani makes eyebrow-raising claim about Netanyahu protests ahead of NYC visit
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu heads to New York City for the U.N. General Assembly as Mayor Zohran Mamdani walks back his earlier protest-related remarks.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday he does not plan to attend protests during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s upcoming visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly, while denying that he has ever encouraged New Yorkers to protest the Israeli leader. The comments come less than two months after Mamdani said New Yorkers had the right to protest Netanyahu’s visit and that he would leave the decision to them. "I do not have any plans to attend any protest at the UNGA," Mamdani said on Wednesday. "To New Yorkers I have never encouraged them to protest. What I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in this city." ISRAEL'S AMBASSADOR SAYS NYC’S MAMDANI IS ‘SOWING CHAOS’ AHEAD OF NETANYAHU’S UN APPEARANCE Mamdani and Netanyahu have clashed over the Israeli leader’s expected New York visit since July, when Mamdani said he had asked his administration to review applicable law to determine whether the city could execute an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against Netanyahu. The Democratic socialist mayor said in July that New Yorkers had the right to protest Netanyahu’s visit, calling protest "one of the bedrocks of our city." ISRAELI UN ENVOY BLASTS MAMDANI AS 'CLOWN' OVER CALL TO ARREST NETANYAHU: 'IT'S A STUNT' "It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special, that New Yorkers can express themselves whether they are in support or in opposition no matter on whatever topic," he said during the press conference on July 22. NETANYAHU ACCUSES MAMDANI OF 'FOMENTING HATE,' SAYS RHETORIC IS MAKING NEW YORK JEWS AFRAID "And I’ve always said that when we respect our Constitution, we also respect our First Amendment. And here in New York City it will always be a place where you can exercise that," the Mayor added. Mamdani has repeatedly criticized Israel’s conduct in Gaza and accused the country of committing genocide, while voicing support for pro-Palestinian causes. He also skipped New York City’s annual Israel Day Parade on May 31, becoming the first mayor in decades to miss the event.
